html:
A manual of war written in Greek in the late 6th century and usually credited to the emperor Maurice, who ruled from 582 to 602, or to a general close to him. It sums up what the eastern Roman army had learned in decades of fighting on many fronts.

Its twelve books cover training, drill, marching, camps and, above all, cavalry. The ideal soldier is a horseman armed with both bow and lance, a lesson taken from the steppe peoples. It contains the first clear mention in a European text of the stirrup, copied from the Avars.

One book describes the enemies of the day and how to fight each:

  • the Persians, disciplined and good at sieges;
  • the Avars and Turks, steppe horsemen best fought in open country;
  • the Franks and Lombards, brave but reckless in a charge;
  • the Slavs, who fought from forests and marshes.
